facts.text: The little egret is a small white heron with a slender black beak, long black legs and yellow feet.
facts.quote: It is a white bird with a slender black beak, long black legs and, in the western race, yellow feet.

facts.text: In the breeding season it grows two long plumes on its nape that form a crest.
facts.quote: In the breeding season, the adult has two long plumes on the nape that form a crest.

facts.text: During courtship, its lores turn red and the feet of yellow-footed races also turn red.
facts.quote: During the height of courtship, the lores turn red and the feet of the yellow-footed races turn red.

facts.text: It is mostly silent, giving croaking and bubbling calls at breeding colonies and a harsh alarm call when disturbed.
facts.quote: Little egrets are mostly silent but make various croaking and bubbling calls at their breeding colonies and produce a harsh alarm call when disturbed.

facts.text: It hunts by shuffling its feet to stir up small fish, running with raised wings, or standing still to ambush prey.
facts.quote: they stalk their prey in shallow water, often running with raised wings or shuffling their feet to disturb small fish, or may stand still and wait to ambush prey.

facts.text: Besides fish, it eats amphibians, reptiles, mammals, birds, crustaceans, insects, spiders and worms.
facts.quote: Their diet is mainly fish, but amphibians, small reptiles, mammals and birds are also eaten, as well as crustaceans, molluscs, insects, spiders and worms.

facts.text: Pairs defend a small breeding territory of about 3 to 4 metres around the nest.
facts.quote: Pairs defend a small breeding territory, usually extending around 3 to 4 m (10 to 13 ft) from the nest.

facts.text: It has colonised the New World, first being seen in Barbados in 1954 and beginning to breed there in 1994.
facts.quote: The first record there was on Barbados in April 1954. The bird began breeding on the island in 1994 and now also breeds in the Bahamas.
